Essay draft · September 2026

Why I still build robots for humans

I believe that robots will live and work alongside us. During my PhD, I wanted to make that future concrete enough for people to encounter.

I began my doctorate in 2022. Over the following years, the capabilities of AI systems changed remarkably quickly. For someone coming from human–machine systems and human factors, it was easy to feel that every working prototype was already a generation behind.

But a newer model was only part of what I needed. I needed a robot that could see a board, move a piece, respond to a person, and keep the interaction going. I needed people to be able to walk alongside a robot and discover what felt natural, or confusing, about directing it. I needed students to see an AI-generated plan become a trajectory, with consequences they could inspect.

Making an encounter possible

Building a system for an experiment involves choices. A component may be less recent but easier to verify. A constrained task may reveal more than an impressive demonstration. An interface may need to make failure visible, even when hiding it would make the system look more capable.

OpenChessRobot gave me a way to study these choices in one complete system. Chess offered a state that could be checked, actions that could be executed, and explanations that could be compared with expert judgment. A fluent explanation did not always contain the strategic understanding it seemed to promise.

The visual-search study raised a related question at an earlier processing stage. Humans and models could agree on which conditions were difficult while producing very different response patterns. Similar outcomes were not sufficient evidence of similar perception.

Following the question upstream

These projects led me to think about interaction through perception, cognition and response. Where does the mismatch begin? What evidence would help a person detect it? Who should take over which part of the task?

I now want to ask more of these questions from the robot’s side. Could a system recognize that a failed task needs a new observation, a different plan, or a correction to execution? Could it propose a test that distinguishes these possibilities? Could the outcome change what it chooses to investigate next?

That is the connection I see between my work in HRI and my interest in embodied intelligence and scientific agents. The ambition is continuous: understand what it takes for intelligent machines to work alongside people, and build the mechanisms that make it possible.

My next experiment will start on a smaller, measurable problem: whether an agent can improve its experimental strategy. I want to evaluate the quality of its evidence, the experiments it repeats unnecessarily, and whether anything it learns carries over to a new task.

The robot still matters. It keeps the question attached to a world where an explanation, a decision and an action must eventually meet.

Draft for author review. Grounded in the supplied thesis Chapters 1–6 and the accompanying research statement.
